title: AST SpaceMobile to build its own 20-ton “Blacklift” rockets with Firefly Aerospace engines
html:
Satellite direct-to-device (D2D) company AST SpaceMobile is to make its own launch rockets to send its satellites into orbit.

The company has announced it will build its own custom reusable 20-ton rocket called Blacklift to deploy its BlueBird satellites into low Earth orbit, five at a time, using Miranda and Vira engines developed by Firefly Aerospace.

AST aims to deploy more than 100 BlueBird satellites cumulatively between 2027 and 2028, and hopes to be using Blacklift by late 2028.

“The Blacklift rocket is the springboard to significantly expand our total addressable market, providing AST SpaceMobile with regular unconstrained access to orbit and providing for the most favorable owners’ economics in the industry,” said Abel Avellan, founder, chairman, and CEO of AST SpaceMobile. “This will accelerate our mission to build a new layer of global connectivity, extending connectivity beyond terrestrial networks and helping to bring AI-enabled services wherever people live, work and travel.”

Midland, Texas-based AST has agreed to pay $800 million in upfront consideration to Firefly, comprised of $400 million in cash and 10-to-14 million shares of Class A Common Stock. Additionally, AST will pay $250 million for the delivery of Firefly’s engines to equip Blacklift’s first three launches and a further $250 million over a three-year period for engineering support.

Since Texas neighbor SpaceX stressed the power of verticalization in its IPO document, the space tech industry and its investor base have become particularly convinced of the strategy.

Verticalization nation

Scott Wisniewski, president at AST, said Blacklift will expand the company’s applications beyond D2D into radar and secure comms for the US Government specifically, as well as Internet of things (IoT), federal emergency, AI Edge compute, and more.

AST leans on the phrase “flight-proven” in its language concerning Firefly’s technology. Firefly’s Miranda engine has performed over 175 hot fire tests, which the company equates to 20 full first-stage flights. Miranda has never flown on a live rocket test, but has also been lined up for the hotly anticipated Antares 330 medium-lift rocket developed by Northrop Grumman.

Firefly stresses its launch credentials in the statement by citing its small-lift Alpha (Firefly α) rocket, a rocket that has flown seven times, flying successfully on three occasions, deploying seven satellites nominally in its history, using four of its “Reaver” first-stage engines.

Wisniewski claimed the engine would allow AST to “leapfrog” the usual 5-10 year development cycle of a space rocket. While engines are an excruciatingly tricky detail in proving out a successful rocket, they represent just a fraction of all that can go wrong in launch.

The new space race

Successful launchers such as SpaceX, Rocket Lab, Ariane, and China have all spent around a decade iterating rocket technology, starting out small. Firefly has invested in that long technological ascent, and appears to be trekking through some of its more punishing years today. Historically, attempts by space agencies and aerospace companies to “leapfrog” toward premium launch products have been misadventures.

Orbital Data center developer Cowboy Space had a similar idea in late October with the announcement of its medium-lift “Big Iron” rocket that transforms into a data center.

AST’s strategy may have more to do with necessity than good business sense.

SpaceX has committed to “winding down” the Falcon 9, likely because developing and operating a first-rate rocket and offering it affordably has been loss-making for the company. Experts suggest the Falcon 9 will not fly commercially after 2028, after which we can only speculate what will happen to the world’s most successful rocket.

In April this year, AST lost seven BlueBird satellites after a partial failure of Jeff Bezos-owned Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket, which influenced a $2 billion slump in its market cap.

In late October, Analysis Mason, a veteran market analysis firm for the space and satellite industry, drew attention to the scale of the coming launch bottleneck. In the firm's "bold statements for space" presentation, first conducted at WSBW 2026 in Paris, analysts predicted that a supply squeeze will prevent 200,000 satellites, representing an estimated $210bn in manufacturing value, from flying up to 2035, even assuming the success of SpaceX “super heavy-lift” Starship rocket.

"The satellite launch bottleneck is not a new problem, and operators are soon going to face significant challenges deploying their constellations at all, let alone on time,” claimed Dallas Kasaboski, research director at Analysis Mason.
summary: Commits $1.3bn to engines for new proprietary rocket, reckons it’ll be good to go in two years
